extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students (first-year math course peers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing clear, well-structured mathematical solutions/proofs targeted primarily at first-year undergraduate students; focuses on how to present calculations and deductions as a convincing argument. Covers sentence/paragraph structure, justification of steps, and self-checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solution as an argument
rubrics_metrics.description: A solution to a math problem is an argument. Therefore, it should be phrased and structured in the same way as an argument, with the intent to convince the reader of a certain idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat solutions like essays: everything you write should work toward convincing the reader of the thesis. Organize content and style together so that the structure mirrors the argument you want to make.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish content from style
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of a solution consists of the calculations or deductions you perform; style is how those phrases are joined into sentences and paragraphs so the argument is easy to follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content (calculations/deductions) is what you learn in lectures; style is how you present it. Good style is required: poor style can make correct content unreadable and irrelevant to the reader/grader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target audience / explanation level
rubrics_metrics.description: Your choice of target audience determines how much explanation is required; for a first-year mathematics course, write with your peers as the audience and explain each of your deductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume the reader is a peer in the course: do not omit justifications you expect they cannot trivially supply. When in doubt include more detail rather than less: 'you cannot include too much detail' for first-year work.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the thesis clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Every argument has a thesis: the main point of your argument. Usually the thesis statement is determined by the question you are answering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the conclusion or the statement to be proved explicit (often it is the problem statement). Ensure all subsequent statements aim to justify that thesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical flow should mirror reading order
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure of the argument should mirror the logical flow: write so the reader reads premises and justifications top-to-bottom in the same direction as your deductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with statements that are clearly true and proceed to direct consequences, ending with the thesis. Avoid presenting the argument 'from conclusion backwards' (i.e., starting with the claim and showing the justification later), as in the initial √ab example; reorganize so each line follows from the previous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sentences and connectives (link phrases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equations and inequalities are phrases; join them into sentences with words like 'because', 'thus', 'since', or implication symbols. Do not present only a list of isolated phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the logical connection between lines explicit by inserting words or punctuation. Single long sentences are acceptable in math if the logical connection is clear, but the connection must be readable and justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify nontrivial steps and state used theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: If the justification for a phrase includes anything beyond the truth of the previous phrase, you must explicitly state that justification (e.g., cite the theorem or reasoning enabling a step).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: when simplifying expressions in a limit you must state the theorem that allows replacing f(x) by g(x) near a point (not necessarily at the point). Explicitly say 'since ...' and cite the condition/theorem used so the reader sees the justification (limit example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat equations grammatically
rubrics_metrics.description: An equation (or inequality) is a phrase with a subject (left-hand side), a verb (is, is less than), and an object (right-hand side). Present equations so they read as parts of sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punctuate and integrate mathematical expressions into sentence structure to avoid strings of disconnected symbols that are hard to read aloud or follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph unity: single topic per paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: Each paragraph should be about a single topic. For multi-part problems, use separate paragraphs for different subtopics (e.g., zeros, asymptotes, derivative, second derivative when sketching a curve).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize longer solutions into paragraphs by topic; this helps the reader follow which deductions belong together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concluding paragraph for multi-paragraph solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: If your argument requires more than one paragraph, end with a concluding paragraph which summarizes your results and presents the final answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the final paragraph to tie together intermediate results and state the final conclusion (e.g., present the actual sketch after separate analytic paragraphs).

rubrics_metrics.name: State method and outline when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: If the method is not specified (e.g., you choose induction), begin by stating the method (e.g., 'We will prove by induction') and, if the method is complicated, summarize the steps so the reader knows what is going on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For method-driven problems, explicitly announce the approach and provide a short roadmap when necessary so the reader can follow the larger structure of the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-check checklist (post-writing questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: After writing your solution, re-read it and ask: Is each paragraph about a single topic? Is each paragraph made up of complete, properly punctuated sentences? Does each phrase follow logically from the one before it? Is each logical leap justified? Does the progression from one phrase to the next match the argument you are trying to make?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist to catch omissions or unclear steps before submission. These five explicit questions are presented as a compact evaluation rubric to ensure clarity and correctness of exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read your solution aloud
rubrics_metrics.description: Try reading your solution aloud to find errors and omissions; many issues become apparent when spoken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading aloud helps detect disconnected phrases, missing justifications, and grammatical problems. It's a quick technique to improve clarity before submitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about domain/definition issues when manipulating expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: When manipulating algebraic expressions you must be careful about domain issues (e.g., canceling factors that are zero at a point). Make the necessary conditions explicit so the reader understands why the step is valid (as in the limit example where expressions are not defined at x=1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state assumptions like 'a,b>0' when needed and note where expressions are undefined; when using limits, cite the theorem that justifies replacing functions on punctured neighborhoods.
